analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage to $5.15 an hour while carving out commute-time pay, tip credits, and teen and computer-worker exemptions.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 281-144 on May 23, 1996, then set it aside and attached its text to a separate small-business bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill began as a measure letting employers avoid paying wages for time workers spend driving company vehicles to and from work. When it reached the House floor, it had been rewritten to also raise the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 an hour, then to $5.15 a year later — the first increase in five years. Along the way, it picked up exemptions for employers: a revised tip credit for restaurants, a lower starting wage for workers under 20 in their first 90 days, and an overtime exemption for well-paid computer professionals. The House passed it on May 23, 1996, and immediately folded its text into a separate small-business bill (H.R. 3448) for further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage, who would see $4.25 rise to $4.75 within weeks of passage and $5.15 after one year. Workers under 20 and tipped employees gain less than the headline suggests, since the bill lets employers pay them less. Employers using company vehicles also gain, because commute time is no longer compensable.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.75 per hour for the year beginning June 30, 1996, and to $5.15 after that year.

Narrows an employer pay exemption so it only covers commute time in company vehicles within the normal commuting area, and only when the employer and the employee or the employee's representative agree to it.
Guarantees workers under 20 at least $4.25 an hour during their first 90 days, rather than a lower training wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in low-wage industries bear the higher payroll costs, some of which are passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through reduced hours. Workers who drive employer-owned vehicles lose the right to be paid for commuting time. Tipped-restaurant operators can count more tips against the wage floor, and teen workers can legally be paid $4.25 for 90 days.

drawbacks.text: Employers no longer owe minimum wage or overtime for time employees spend driving company vehicles to and from work, removing compensable hours from those workers.
Employers may pay workers under 20 as little as $4.25 an hour during their first 90 days, even after the new minimum takes effect.
Revised tip-credit rules let employers count more employee tips toward the minimum wage, reducing the cash wage tipped workers are guaranteed.
Computer professionals earning at least $27.63 an hour are exempted from both minimum wage and overtime requirements.

A good-faith objection supporters would acknowledge: the wage floor raises costs for small businesses, which some argue reduces entry-level hiring or hours — Republicans on the floor pushed an amendment to exempt businesses with under $500,000 in annual sales from the minimum wage entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a first minimum wage increase since 1991, lifting pay for millions of workers — outweighs the costs for most people, and the increase is modest and phased in over two steps. But the bill is noticeably weaker than a clean wage increase: the commuting pay exemption restores a loss for a specific group of workers, the 90-day youth subminimum and expanded tip credit trim protections, and the computer-professional exemption removes overtime from a defined group. It is a genuine wage raise wrapped in employer accommodations that were the price of passage.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 281-144, then laid it on the table and attached its text to a separate small-business bill (H.R. 3448), which carried the provisions forward — the bill itself never moved independently.

narrative.text: Rep. Harris Fawell introduced the bill on March 14, 1995, originally as a measure relieving employers of liability for failing to pay wages for employee use of employer-owned vehicles for commuting.

The bill was referred to the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, which forwarded it by voice vote in December 1995; the full committee ordered it reported amended by voice vote on March 21, 1996.
The committee-reported version narrowed the commuting exemption to apply only within the employer's normal commuting area and only when the employer and the employee or employee representative agree.
The Rules Committee paired consideration of H.R. 1227 with H.R. 3448, and the House considered the bill under that rule on May 22-23, 1996.
On May 23, 1996, the House agreed 267-161 to a motion to consider the Riggs amendment; Democrats backed it 190-5 while most Republicans opposed taking it up.

Debate included the Goodling amendment, which the rule divided so the question was split between several provisions and a section exempting businesses with gross annual sales under $500,000 from the minimum wage.
The House passed the amended bill 281-144: Democrats 187-6 in favor, Republicans 93-138 against, the lone Independent in favor.
Immediately after passage, the House laid the bill on the table and appended its text to H.R. 3448, directing further action to that bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Both low-wage workers, who were on the way to a raise, and employers, who won the commuting, tip-credit, youth, and computer-professional carve-outs — the House packaged them together and moved the package into H.R. 3448.

for.name: Rep. Harris W. Fawell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as a commute-time pay measure, and its reported version carried the two-step minimum wage increase to $4.75 and $5.15.

for.name: 187 of 197 House Democrats
for.role: House Democrats voting on final passage

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed Congress throughout 1996 to raise the federal minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.15, making it a signature issue of his re-election campaign.

against.name: 138 of 235 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans voting on final passage

against.name: Rep. William Goodling
against.role: U.S. Representative (PA), sponsor of the Goodling amendment
against.what_they_did: Offered an amendment package on the floor that included a provision exempting small businesses with gross annual sales under $500,000 from the minimum wage.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed final passage nearly unanimously (187-6), while a majority of House Republicans opposed it (93-138 against); the bill still passed 281-144 because Democratic support outweighed the Republican no-votes.

industries.note: They must pay the new $4.75, then $5.15, wage floor, raising payroll costs for their lowest-paid staff — the very workers who benefit. The industry pushed instead for a broad small-business exemption, which was debated but not included in the passed version.

industries.industry: Trucking, delivery, utilities and other employers using company vehicles
industries.note: The bill's original purpose: they no longer owe minimum wage or overtime for employees' commuting time in company vehicles, wiping out compensable hours for those workers.
Revised tip-credit rules let them count more tips against the higher minimum wage, lowering the cash wage they must guarantee tipped workers.
Computer professionals paid at least $27.63 an hour are exempt from minimum wage and overtime rules, cutting overtime costs for employers of programmers and systems analysts.
